title: Notebook investigations for explorEDA
methodology: Actual analysis pages were opened and inspected in their rendered state. Screenshots are captures of those pages, not gallery thumbnails or generated mockups. Some captures show a revealed solution, changed control, or later analytical step; captions identify those states.

Observable source was inspected through visible cells and, where useful, archived exports of the author's notebook source checked against the live page. An archived revision is identified when used. Search snippets alone were not treated as evidence.

Observable's visible JavaScript was inspected as evidence of source methods. Equivalent expressions, queries and chart configurations may reproduce those methods; these references do not imply that explorEDA needs a general JavaScript runtime.

Data availability distinguishes a working live attachment/table, an inspected downloadable snapshot, and an upstream source that was linked but not independently retrieved. Exact formulas are described only when supported by visible source or documented methods.

Observed controls are labeled separately from proposed explorEDA controls. Every compatibility statement is a hypothesis based on the supplied capabilities; explorEDA itself was not inspected. Effort ratings are relative scope judgments, not schedules.

Two retained notebooks have localized execution failures: Bratenahl's sensitivity output and two spatial-tutorial cells. Their functioning analytical sequences and visible methods remain useful; the failures and reproduction limits are specified in their entries.

examples.title: Plot Exploration: Penguins
examples.pattern: Raw observations → grouped comparison → faceted distributions → summary overlay

screenshots.caption: Question 2, with its solution expanded: the prose motivates species as a grouping variable, editable calculation/configuration text precedes the scatterplot, and the next question follows vertically.
screenshots.crop_note: Browser side margins cropped; page content is unchanged.

screenshots.caption: The next analytical step retains species color while adding sex facets. The visible definition and complete output share the reading column. The unlabeled third facet contains observations with missing sex.
screenshots.crop_note: Browser side margins cropped; page content is unchanged.

examples.story: The notebook investigates how penguin body measurements vary by species, sex and island. A raw mass-versus-flipper relationship becomes more informative when species color and then sex facets are added; later questions compare counts, weight distributions and medians. In the inspected charts, longer flippers tend to accompany greater mass, and the groups separate differently across the comparisons. That is our visual interpretation. The author supplies questions and executable solutions rather than a concluding biological claim. This is a guided investigation using real research data, so it is strongest as a small, progressive reproduction, with the pedagogical character stated explicitly.
examples.prose_role: Each question gives the preceding result a reason to change: first relate two measurements, then distinguish species without discarding the relationship, then add sex without losing the species encoding. Later prose motivates counting, binning and median overlays. Hints explain the calculation or encoding; interpretation is largely left to the reader. The notebook therefore demonstrates a sequence of analytical decisions more strongly than a finished computational essay.

data.origin: Kristen Gorman and Palmer Station Long Term Ecological Research; the Palmer Penguins dataset distributed by Allison Horst and colleagues, with a notebook-specific CSV attachment.
data.grain: One measured penguin; 344 records spanning Adelie, Chinstrap and Gentoo penguins on Biscoe, Dream and Torgersen islands in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. Canonical provenance covers 2007–2009; the notebook attachment omits year.
data.fields: species, island, bill_length, bill_depth, flipper_length, body_mass and sex. Lengths are millimeters; mass is grams. The attachment uses MALE/FEMALE and blank sex values, and removes unit suffixes from column names. The canonical CSV retains year, _mm/_g suffixes and lowercase sex values.
calculations: The attachment loads with typed CSV parsing. No explicit row-cleaning step precedes the inspected comparisons. Missing measurements and sex need an explicit policy in a reproduction; the sex-faceted solution visibly retains a blank category.
Questions 1–3 use raw observations: x = flipper_length, y = body_mass; Question 2 adds fill and hover title = species; Question 3 keeps those encodings and facets horizontally by sex.
Question 4 groups by species and counts records for a bar chart. Question 5 repeats species counts within island facets; an alternative uses x = island, y = species and radius = count.

Question 6 bins body_mass and counts rows using Plot.binX with thresholds: 20. Questions 7–8 facet these histograms by sex horizontally and species vertically. The threshold is a requested bin parameter; do not assume it guarantees exactly twenty rendered bins under the library's defaults.
Question 8 overlays a full-height median tick on each sex/species distribution using Plot.groupZ({x: 'median'}, {x: 'body_mass'}), within the existing facet context.

Question 9 asks how many females exceed the lightest male. Its supplied solution shows male extrema, female median and individual observations by species. It does not produce the requested count, so an exact numerical answer would be an extension rather than an observed output.
data.dependencies: The shared data table feeds every chart. The analytical dependency is progressive—each comparison motivates the next—but the original chart cells generally repeat their definitions rather than consuming the preceding chart's output. Within the statistics chart, the histogram counts and median reducer share the same raw rows and facet groups.
data.reproducibility: The actual attachment link, loaded table and visible solution definitions are sufficient for the core reproduction. Data provenance is public and documented. The canonical CSV is an accessible substitute if the attachment fails: rename columns, normalize sex values and preserve missingness. This changes schema preparation, not the intended sample, but identity with the attachment should be checked before claiming a byte-for-byte match.
data.caveats: This is a teaching investigation, with fewer authored conclusions than the journalism examples. Native table sorting and row selection are visible, but no source dependency links the table selection to the charts. Hint/Solution toggles change presentation; they are not analytical filters. The exact Question 9 count is absent.

sequence: Introduce the measured penguins → load and inspect rows → establish fields and missing values.
Ask whether heavier birds have longer flippers → configure a raw scatter → inspect the association.
Ask whether species explain the pattern → add species color and hover labels → compare clusters.
Ask about sex while retaining species → facet the same scatter by sex → compare within groups.
Ask how sample composition varies → count species, then species within islands → inspect bars or a count table.
Ask about weight distributions → bin mass by sex/species → overlay group medians → inspect overlap and formulate the next question.

Sorting; selection need not filter charts

Hover title observed; visual encoding edits proposed
Raw data; changes to this definition remain local
Essential for grouped comparison: sex facets
Same rows and scatter definition; sex
Horizontal facet = sex; retain species colors and common axes
Female, male and missing-sex panels within one chart block
Same data and field policy as prior scatter
Group by species; count rows; optionally facet by island
Species bars and island comparisons; consistent color legend

Bin, facet and overlay edits proposed
Counts and medians must share grouping and filters

fit.minimum: Reproduce Questions 1–3 with the data table: a mass/flipper scatter, a second block adding species color, and a third adding sex facets, joined by the original analytical questions. This is a small first proof. Counts and a histogram-plus-median can extend it when grouped calculations are ready.
fit.compatible: Tables, interactive charts, filters, calculated fields and saved state appear sufficient for much of the exploration, based only on the product description. No arbitrary JavaScript execution is implied by these requirements.
fit.investigate: Facets with shared scales, grouped counts and medians, histogram bin defaults, overlay marks, explicit missing-category behavior, and whether copied or derived chart definitions preserve common configuration without coupling every later edit.
fit.roundtrip: Visual changes to x/y fields, species color, sex or island facet, category order, opacity, hover fields, axis units, bin thresholds and median overlays should update the defining text. A switch from raw observations to counts must update the calculation as well as the chart encoding. The text should expose the grouping and denominator, not merely record cosmetic changes.
fit.scope: The original exposes table inspection and solution toggles, not a shared analytical filter. A proposed global species filter would affect every dependent result; changing one chart's color or facet should remain local unless the text explicitly shares that setting. Histogram and median layers need identical group/filter scope.
fit.lesson: This tests whether users can express a familiar calculation/visual combination in text, refine it with graphical controls, and read a meaningful sequence afterward. It also tests the distinction between a shared dataset, a copied chart definition and a true dependent calculation. Missing values must remain legible when a visual edit introduces a facet.

comparison.data_availability: Exact attachment and canonical public CSV; live rows verified
comparison.calculation_transparency: High: visible solution code; final requested count not supplied
comparison.interaction_complexity: Low: hover, table inspection and disclosure; editing is central
comparison.reproduction_effort: Low for three progressive scatters; medium with facets, bins and overlays

examples.title: What’s different? Analyzing Time-Series Forecast Performance
examples.authors: Zan Armstrong, Mike Freeman and Ian Johnson
examples.pattern: Actual versus forecast → signed difference → event-window investigation

screenshots.caption: The analytical turning point: prose defines the signed difference between actuals and forecast, the chart plots that calculated quantity against a zero baseline, and the next paragraph interprets the result.
screenshots.crop_note: Browser side margins cropped; page content is unchanged.

screenshots.caption: Later in the same reading sequence, the residual calculation is reused in an event-window zoom; the prose interprets two pre-blackout dips.
screenshots.crop_note: Browser side margins cropped; page content is unchanged.

examples.story: The notebook investigates hourly Texas demand around the February 2021 power crisis. Subtracting the forecast from actual demand makes two dips before the rolling blackouts noticeable. This is a particularly clear example of an analytical argument produced by changing what is calculated and displayed. It does not establish why those early dips occurred; price is offered as a follow-up hypothesis.
examples.prose_role: The prose introduces an apparent comparison problem, asks whether demand was above or below forecast, explains the signed difference, interprets the pre-event pattern, and motivates a closer date window. The later diagrams explain why comparing two sloping lines can obscure that difference.

data.origin: U.S. Energy Information Administration Open Data, an ERCOT/Texas hourly demand and day-ahead-forecast snapshot downloaded in August 2021 and attached in September 2021.
data.grain: One hourly observation in Texas/ERCOT, January–February 2021; the live raw and renamed arrays contain 1,417 rows. The fixed event-window subset contains 216 rows.
data.fields: date (UTC timestamp), demand renamed actuals, and forecast. The chart labels demand in MWh, but some explanatory text uses kW; retain raw values and reconcile this source labeling inconsistency rather than applying an invented conversion.
calculations: Parse the attached CSV with typed fields; rename demand to actuals.
Compute signed difference actuals − forecast; positive and negative values receive consistent orange and purple encodings.
Represent rolling blackouts at 2021-02-15T07:25:00Z (1:25 a.m. CST). Filter the zoom from 2021-02-07T07:25:00Z through 2021-02-16T07:25:00Z inclusively.

The source derives daily/weekly ticks from UTC intervals shifted six hours to show Central time, and derives maxima for chart/annotation placement (maxDelta 10,436 and maxValue 76,783 in the inspected state).
data.dependencies: Typed data → renamed relation → actual/forecast line charts and residual charts. The zoom predicate produces a smaller relation reused by later line and residual comparisons. Shared event and semantic-color definitions feed multiple graphics and explanatory annotations.
data.reproducibility: The live loaded rows, downloadable attachment link, visible transformation definitions and stated subtraction are enough for the analytical core. The attachment bytes were not independently downloaded. A failed browser download did not prevent the notebook itself from loading and displaying the data.
data.caveats: Unit labels are inconsistent; do not preserve them uncritically. The event window is a fixed authored filter, not a reader-operated brush. The early demand decline is an observed temporal relationship, not a demonstrated cause. Missing-value and duplicate-hour handling were not independently audited; an exact match should make those policies explicit.

sequence: Introduce the forecast question → inspect hourly actual/forecast values → show two lines and blackout annotation.
Explain the desired comparison → derive actuals minus forecast → show signed differences around zero.
Interpret the unexpected pre-blackout dips → filter to the nine-day event window → show the enlarged residual pattern → propose a follow-up question.
elements: Explain signed error and connect each result to the next question
Prose before and after each output
Interpretations refer to residual and zoom results
x=time; y=demand; two labeled colored lines; vertical event rule
x=time; y=difference; zero baseline; orange above, purple below
Inclusive date filter; same difference encoding; callouts for pre-event dips
Fixed authored window; an editable date control would be an addition
Derived subset feeds later residual and line comparisons
Optional: perception diagrams and filled bands
Fill between lines; authored explanatory illustrations
Can be omitted without losing the investigation

fit.minimum: Keep the introduction, original two-line chart, explicit residual calculation, signed-error plot and nine-day zoom with interpretation. The conceptual cartoons and repeated return to the original chart are optional.
fit.compatible: Calculated fields, filters, interactive chart definitions, tables and saved analysis state appear to cover the core, based only on the product description.
fit.investigate: Shared named calculations across blocks; positive/negative rule or bar encodings; event and text annotations; a clear distinction between display-domain edits and upstream date filtering; consistent units and semantic colors.
fit.roundtrip: Graphical changes to mark type, axis fields and limits, color assignments, event position/label, annotation text and window bounds should update the relevant block text. Changing a residual chart’s visual style should preserve the subtraction it depends on.
fit.scope: There are no main reader controls in the inspected notebook. The authored event filter affects the zoomed branch, while the complete series remains available above.
fit.lesson: A small calculation can be the analytical turning point. This tests whether two-way editing preserves a named derived field, reuses it in a later block, and records local view changes without accidentally changing the evidence above.

comparison.calculation_transparency: High; explicit subtraction and fixed date filter
comparison.interaction_complexity: Low; authored views, no main reader controls

examples.title: What caused this? An analysis adventure
examples.authors: Ian Johnson, Zan Armstrong and Mike Freeman
examples.pattern: Aggregate anomaly → category decomposition → shared-scale comparisons

screenshots.caption: The opening anomaly: a concrete question, the total-generation chart, and prose proposing a more granular data source.
screenshots.crop_note: Browser side margins cropped; page content is unchanged.

screenshots.caption: The later decomposition: prose explains the need for common scales, followed by fuel-type facets using the same hourly records.
screenshots.crop_note: Browser side margins cropped; page content is unchanged.

examples.story: A fictional analyst investigates a spike in real Texas generation data. Successive views show a two-week episode, not just one high day: a coal plateau, a nuclear dip, sustained lower wind generation, and a large rise in natural-gas generation. The epilogue explicitly says the aggregate patterns cannot determine which fuel is intrinsically better or worse or by themselves establish the crisis mechanism.
examples.prose_role: The story gives each chart a reason to exist: confirm the total, identify contributing categories, address overlapping lines, examine stacking, and finally separate fuel types with comparable scales. Interpretation then accompanies each selected fuel panel.

data.origin: EIA Open Data hourly net generation by fuel for the Texas region; a cached API response deliberately attached so the article remains reproducible.

links.label: EIA grid monitor used for fuel colors

data.grain: One fuel category × UTC hour in January–February 2021, Texas region. The live transformed array has 9,912 rows, covering seven fuels: coal, natural gas, nuclear, other, solar, hydro and wind.
data.fields: series_id/id, series name/name, derived type, parsed UTC date, and value. The y-axis divides values by 1,000. Source labels vary between thousand megawatts and thousand megawatt hours per day; the facet code uses hourly rows directly, so a daily-total interpretation is unsupported.
calculations: Load cached JSON; flatten each series’ date/value pairs; extract fuel type from the series name; parse %Y%m%dT%HZ as UTC; sort by date.
The total-generation line bins by UTC hour and sums value across fuel records. Its opening variant applies a window with k=1, which does not smooth the data.
Later fuel lines and stacked areas map the same date/value rows with type determining grouping and color. Faceting splits by type while retaining a common y scale.
Selected-fuel panels highlight the February 7–21 episode. Exact styling/shading helper logic was not fully inspected; the underlying fuel comparison and scale transforms were visible.
data.dependencies: One cleaned long relation feeds the total aggregation, fuel lines, stacked areas, facets and individual fuel views. A shared semantic fuel-color mapping also supports colored phrases in the prose.
data.reproducibility: The cached 215KB JSON link, populated table, visible load/cleaning source, and inspected chart definitions support the core reproduction. Bytes were not independently downloaded. Reproducing the original obsolete EIA API URL is unnecessary because the frozen attachment is present.
data.caveats: The source’s hourly-versus-daily and power-versus-energy wording should be resolved explicitly. The notebook decomposes measured generation; it is not a causal model of generation failures, unmet demand or fuel reliability. Missing-value and duplicate-hour handling were not independently audited; an exact match should make those policies explicit.

sequence: Receive an anomaly question → acquire detailed hourly fuel data → inspect the records.
Sum fuel categories per hour → reproduce the total line → ask what contributes.
Split lines by fuel → try stacked area → explain why overlap and moving baselines hinder comparison.
Facet with common scales → inspect selected fuels in separate full-width panels → interpret the two-week episode and state causal limits.

Single total line with anomaly label

Facet rows by type; shared y-domain; area or line marks; ordered fuel labels
Preserves common data and scale semantics

Specific findings attached to each fuel

fit.minimum: Keep the anomaly, source table, hourly total, category lines and fuel facets, followed by the four short findings. An initial reproduction can omit the fictional office framing, stack intermediate and custom highlight styling.
fit.compatible: Grouping, aggregation, charts, calculated fields and filters appear compatible with the described capabilities; this remains a hypothesis.
fit.investigate: Common-scale faceting, stable category color mappings shared with prose, named aggregate versus detail relations, and preserving independently authored comparisons while editing chart configurations.
fit.roundtrip: Switching total to grouped lines, line to area, stacked to faceted layout, fuel order, scale domain, color or annotation should persist into the block text. Removing grouping is a calculation/configuration change with analytical consequences and should remain explicit.
fit.scope: No analytical reader controls were observed. All panels reuse one dataset with different authored aggregations, grouping or local fuel selections.
fit.lesson: This tests whether visually editing a chart can progressively refine an investigation while keeping prior steps readable and preserving aggregation grain, shared scales and categories.

comparison.calculation_transparency: High for data shaping and chart aggregation; helper polish partly uninspected

examples.title: Discovering Date Patterns
examples.authors: Mike Freeman, Zan Armstrong and Ian Johnson
examples.pattern: Time series → calendar features → grouped distributions

screenshots.caption: The initial investigation: explanatory prose, a rolling-average selector, a date brush and a full-width demand chart. Captured with hourly data selected.
screenshots.crop_note: Browser side margins cropped; page content is unchanged.

screenshots.caption: A later dependent step, captured after changing the vertical grouping to Day. The horizontal grouping remains Quarter; prose, controls, the result and a derived-record inspection stay in one reading sequence.
screenshots.crop_note: Browser side margins cropped; page content is unchanged.

examples.story: The question is how much structure can be discovered from only a timestamp and a measured value. The notebook first smooths California electricity demand, then derives local calendar categories and compares distributions within them. Its reported patterns vary by hour and season; the inspected quarter-by-day view also makes weekday/weekend differences visible. This is an analytical walkthrough with interpretation, rather than a set of unrelated charts.
examples.prose_role: The prose introduces the restricted starting information, explains why smoothing helps, motivates additional date fields, and uses the first results to choose the next comparison. It also distinguishes UTC display time from local calendar time and closes by explaining how the same reasoning transfers to other timestamp/value data.

data.origin: U.S. Energy Information Administration Open Data; an attached California-region hourly-demand snapshot used by the notebook.
data.grain: One California-region hourly demand observation; 8,784 rows for the local 2020 leap year. The final local-hour record is stored as 2021-01-01T07:00Z.
data.fields: date (UTC timestamp) and value (electricity demand, chart-labelled MWh). Derived fields are local hour, day of month, weekday, weekend/weekday, ISO week, month and quarter, using America/Los_Angeles.
calculations: Parse the timestamp and derive calendar features in America/Los_Angeles, preserving the original instant for the time axis.
The rolling transform uses k = 1, 24, 168 or 672 hourly observations. The source delegates alignment and edge handling to its Observable Plot version; those defaults were not independently resolved.
The date brush supplies the line's x-domain and masks points outside the interval. It does not filter the data used by the later grouped output.

The later chart groups raw observations by the two selected calendar categories. Each group displays demand values as ticks and its mean as the colored background; group means also feed tooltips. Weekday and month orders are explicit.
data.dependencies: raw_data → enriched data → inspected table and grouped distributions. enriched data + smoothing choice + brush limits → line chart. Grouping selectors affect the faceted result and tooltip summaries, while the earlier smoothing and brush controls remain local to the line.
data.reproducibility: The live table, attached CSV link and visible/archived authored transformations are sufficient for the core reproduction. The attachment link was inspected and the notebook loaded its rows; the CSV bytes were not independently downloaded. The archive is a preserved revision and was checked against live behavior, not assumed to be the current page wholesale.
data.caveats: Resolve window alignment, edge behavior and sort order explicitly for an exact match. The source uses a PST tooltip label throughout the year despite deriving daylight-saving-aware local fields; a faithful analytical reproduction should label the timezone clearly. This is a labeling issue, not evidence of incorrect local feature derivation. Missing-value and duplicate-hour handling were not independently audited; an exact match should make those policies explicit.

sequence: Explain the timestamp-only question → load and inspect date/value rows.
Define a rolling window and visible date extent → show the time series → interpret daily and seasonal structure.
Explain local calendar features → derive them → display the enriched table.
Choose two grouping dimensions → show demand distributions and group means → compare seasonal and weekday patterns.
elements: Explain UTC versus local time and the purpose of each comparison
Interpretation refers to the relevant result
Parse date; derive America/Los_Angeles calendar fields
Inspectable table with original and derived fields
x=UTC time; y=demand MWh; k-row rolling mean; stable y extent
Enriched rows; horizontal and vertical categories
x=demand; fx/fy=chosen calendar groups; ticks=rows; fill=group mean
Calendar comparison with ordered facets and mean tooltip
Recomputes grouping and means, independent of line controls
Explain how the chosen categories expose another pattern
Must remain associated with its comparison
Callouts illustrating hour and quarter differences
Can be replaced by ordinary text and annotations

fit.minimum: Use the two-column snapshot, a raw-data table, one rolling line and one quarter-by-weekday grouped chart. Keep the text that motivates the move from time to calendar categories. A mean-by-group chart can be an initial simplification, but it should be labeled as losing the distribution information.
fit.compatible: Tables, calculated calendar fields, filters, interactive charts and saved state appear to cover much of this workflow, based only on the supplied product description.
fit.investigate: Timezone-aware date extraction, rolling windows with explicit defaults, two-dimensional facets, per-group distribution marks, and control bindings to a specific result. These are capability questions rather than requirements for arbitrary JavaScript execution.
fit.roundtrip: Changing the smoothing window, axis domain, facet fields, category order, tick opacity, mean color scale, labels or tooltip content should update the corresponding block definition. A facet change that changes aggregation should update both grouping and result configuration, rather than only its visual layout.
fit.scope: Observed controls have different scopes: smoothing and brush are local to the line; the later selectors recompute only grouped comparisons. A future global date filter would be a different, explicitly declared behavior.
fit.lesson: The reading sequence and calculation dependencies are related but not identical. An enriched table can feed separate branches, each with local control state. Two-way editing should preserve those branches and expose defaults such as window size and calendar timezone in text.

comparison.calculation_transparency: High; explicit derivation and grouping; window defaults unresolved
comparison.interaction_complexity: Moderate: brush, rolling and facet selectors

examples.title: Correlation over time
examples.authors: Mike Freeman, Zan Armstrong and Ian Johnson
examples.pattern: Time-aligned join → visual relationship → calendar-conditioned comparisons

screenshots.caption: Prose motivates a month-colored scatterplot and exposes the limitations of overlapping groups; the table from the preceding calculation remains visible at the top.
screenshots.crop_note: Browser side margins cropped; page content is unchanged.

screenshots.caption: A later step after selecting hour: explanation, the control and the beginning of the faceted result. The same overall distribution appears as gray reference marks in every facet.
screenshots.crop_note: Browser side margins cropped; page content is unchanged.

screenshots.caption: The hourly facets continue into an explanation of how each subset compares with the shared reference distribution.
screenshots.crop_note: Browser side margins cropped; page content is unchanged.

examples.story: The notebook asks how the relationship between Texas electricity demand and temperature changes over time. It moves from a crowded colored scatterplot to calendar facets. Its worked interpretation compares 10 a.m. with other hours: demand is relatively higher at low temperatures and lower at high temperatures. The analysis is visual; the current notebook does not calculate a linear correlation coefficient or regression.
examples.prose_role: The prose defines the comparison, explains the join’s geographical assumption, diagnoses occlusion and legend effort, motivates spatial separation, and interprets the shapes against the full-data background.

data.origin: EIA Texas electricity demand and NOAA Dallas/Fort Worth airport weather, downloaded through the authors’ companion notebooks and attached as CSVs.
data.grain: One matched UTC hour from late September 2019 to late September 2021. Live demand contains 17,545 rows; the temperature and joined arrays each contain 17,528. The complete archived weather CSV matching the live attachment hash was inspected, confirming the period.
data.fields: date; value renamed demand (MWh); air_temp renamed temp (°C); precomputed hour, day, weekend, week, month, quarter, daytime and feel. Demand covers Texas while temperature is from one airport.
calculations: Typed-load both CSVs; join on their shared UTC hourly timestamp; rename measured fields and drop series id/name.
Color the scatter by a selected time category. Random drawing order and opacity 0.5 reduce the effect of occlusion.

The faceted view groups by a separately selected category. A constant-gray binned occupancy layer of the entire dataset is repeated in every facet; source bin widths are 1°C and 1,000 MWh. Colored dots show each subset.
Calendar category labels and ordering are explicit; a shared palette feeds both the scatter and facets.
data.dependencies: Joined data feeds the table and both chart branches. One radio controls scatter color grouping; another controls faceting. The palette selector is shared. The gray background deliberately references all joined rows rather than the current facet subset. One finer dependency appears in archived revision 1969: the first scatter category also controls whether the Cividis palette is reversed in the faceted view. That styling dependency was found in source, not tested as a live interaction.
data.reproducibility: The actual controls worked and the join, attachments, schema and preserved source are visible. The archive was checked against the live narrative, data hashes and behavior; it is a pinned revision, not presumed identical to every current UI detail.
data.caveats: The exact cutoffs of precomputed daytime and feel categories were not verified; use the attached columns or restrict a minimum version to explicit hour/month categories. A statewide demand series and one airport temperature series have different geographic scope, an assumption the notebook itself discusses. Missing-value and duplicate-hour handling were not independently audited; an exact match should make those policies explicit. The timezone used to create the attached calendar-category columns was not independently established; use the supplied fields for the reference reproduction. Joined row counts alone do not verify one-to-one matching or identify all unmatched-hour cases.

sequence: Ask about a changing relationship → load and align hourly sources → display the joined table.
Color temperature-versus-demand by a time category → inspect overlap → try alternate palettes.
Separate calendar categories into facets → repeat the full-data gray reference → compare hourly distributions and interpret the 10 a.m. pattern.
elements: Explain time alignment and spatial mismatch
Inner/shared-field join; rename demand/temp; drop id/name
x=temp °C; y=demand MWh; color=time category; opacity 0.5; radius 2
Categorical relationship plot and matching legend
Same x/y; facet=category; gray all-data 1°C×1,000-MWh occupancy bins; colored subset dots
Comparable distributions against a fixed reference
Local facet branch plus full-data reference
Shared color scale; sequential/categorical legend behavior
Updates both charts; archived first-period setting also affects Cividis reversal
Explain relative demand at a given temperature and hour
Static callouts for 5 a.m., 10 a.m. and 6 p.m.

fit.minimum: Join the two attached sources, show a month-colored scatter, then an hourly faceted scatter with an all-data reference and the accompanying interpretation. Four selected hours could be a compact first pass if clearly identified as a subset.
fit.compatible: Tables, interactive encodings, calculated fields, filters and saved state plausibly cover much of this workflow; joins, temporal semantics and faceting must be checked against explorEDA.
fit.investigate: Joining by typed timestamps, separately scoped controls, shared scales and palettes, facet wrapping, reference layers that intentionally ignore facet filtering, and readable large-point rendering.
fit.roundtrip: Changing x/y fields, calendar category, facet layout, category order, palette, opacity, point size, bin width, labels or legend should change the defining text. Switching a chart’s category should also update its grouping and labels rather than leaving stale calculations.
fit.scope: Observed: the hour facet control changes the second result; the first remains month-colored. Source: palette is shared across both charts. Neither radio changes the upstream joined table. The archived source additionally lets the first period selector reverse the faceted Cividis colors when daytime is selected. An exact reproduction should preserve or explicitly revise this secondary styling dependency.
fit.lesson: This tests a shared computed relation with separate interactive branches, plus a background result whose scope differs from the foreground. It also tests whether two-way editing preserves data meaning when calendar grouping changes.

comparison.data_availability: Exact two-file attachments; live rows and matching archived weather bytes
comparison.calculation_transparency: High for join and marks; precomputed category cutoffs partly opaque
comparison.interaction_complexity: Moderate: two radios and shared palette

examples.title: How Bratenahl, Ohio, Disproportionately Targets Black Drivers
examples.authors: Cid Standifer and David Eads / The Marshall Project
examples.pattern: Missing-data sensitivity → grouped rates → association → geographic corroboration

screenshots.caption: The officer comparison places an interpreted grouped table, explanatory prose, a bubble scatter with regression and confidence band, and the next geographic question in one vertical reading sequence.
screenshots.crop_note: Browser side margins cropped; page content is unchanged.

screenshots.caption: A later analytical step joins ticketed drivers' home locations to neighborhood characteristics, then presents successive grouped tables with interpretation. The notebook uses tables here rather than requiring a custom map.
screenshots.crop_note: Browser side margins cropped; page content is unchanged.

examples.story: The investigation asks whether Bratenahl's traffic enforcement disproportionately affects Black drivers and how incomplete race recording changes that assessment. It first examines missing data, then compares recording and race patterns across officers, and finally checks the neighborhoods where ticketed people live. In the rendered geographic tables, 498 of 956 tract-matched ticket records are associated with majority-Black tracts, and 776 with tracts below the stated Ohio median household income. These describe the matched records, not all stops or traffic exposure. The structure works because each section addresses a limitation or alternative explanation raised by the previous one, with prose interpreting the results and introducing a corroborating lens.
examples.prose_role: Prose establishes the reporting question, explains why two administrative sources answer different questions, makes missingness a methodological issue, interprets officer-level comparisons, and motivates geographic corroboration. It closes with reporting checks from court observations and sampled arrest records. This is one of the clearest examples of an argument requiring prose and results to remain in order.

data.origin: Bratenahl police stop records and ticket records obtained by the reporting team, supplemented with geocoded addresses and Census-derived tract attributes. The companion investigation was published by The Marshall Project and Cleveland reporting partners.

links.label: Stops CSV used by the notebook
Geocoded ticket records used by the notebook

data.grain: Stops: 4,048 police stop records, January 1, 2020–September 15, 2022. Tickets: 1,006 ticket records for January 1–September 15, 2022, with geocoded home locations. These are separate sources and grains. No deduplication proving one ticket row equals one unique driver was verified. Scope is Bratenahl enforcement, Ohio, with ticketed people's residences extending beyond the village.
data.fields: Stops use date, loc1/loc2 (cross streets), dispo, sex, race and badge1. B and W are Black and White; blank and U are handled differently in different calculations. Other race codes are present but their meanings were not established in the inspected methods. Tickets contain initiating action and geocoding fields, including Longitude and Latitude in degrees. Public displays omit name/street address fields. Tract attributes include Black and White population percentages and median annual household income in USD.
calculations: Overall missing race: (1,834 blank + 34 U) / 4,048 = 46.15%. The 2022 sensitivity branch filters dates after 2021-12-31, yielding 1,071 stops, and classifies both blank and U as missing: 354 missing, 717 recorded.

Sensitivity control whitePct ranges 0–100 by five, initially 75. For missing-count N, the source adds round(whitePct/100 × N) to White and round((1 − whitePct/100 − 0.01) × N) to Black. Other categories are unchanged; shares divide by the sum of adjusted counts. Although the prose reserves one percent for other categories, the source does not explicitly add that remainder to them. Do not replace this with a denominator of all 1,071 without identifying it as a methodological change.

Officer analysis counts by badge1 and race, pivots race codes into columns, and retains officers with total > 10. total includes blank + A + W + B + F + I + U. pctblack = 100 × B / (A + W + B + F + I + U); pctblank = 100 × blank / total. Thus U remains in the officer Black-share denominator, while the sensitivity branch treats U as missing. The prose's less-than-ten exclusion is slightly different from the actual greater-than-ten inclusion.

The officer scatter uses x = pctblack, y = pctblank, radius = total and hover title = badge number. Plot.linearRegressionY fits the displayed regression with ci: 0.95. The code and rendered confidence band are visible; the fitted coefficient values are not reported.

Ticket coordinates are parsed as numbers and converted to points. Each polygon receives the count returned by turf.pointsWithinPolygon. The tract collection filters attachment records to those with a type property, leaving 3,162 valid features from an array of 3,168.

Tract flags are Black percentage >= 50; White percentage < 50; and median household income < 62,262 USD. Grouped tables sum ticket-point counts and divide each subtotal by the matched total. The inspected majority-Black table is 498/956; the income table is 776/956. Municipality and neighborhood matching have different denominators and should not silently reuse 1,006 or 956.
data.dependencies: Stops → date/missingness subsets → sensitivity estimate → associated percentages and prose. Separately, stops → badge/race counts → pivoted rates → officer table and scatter. Tickets → coordinate points + polygons → polygon counts → demographic flags/grouped shares → interpreted geography tables. The branches share some sources but are not one linear execution chain.
data.reproducibility: The notebook successfully loads raw tables, the officer graph and geographic summaries; the source CSV URLs and tract attachment were inspected. These are sufficient for a focused officer comparison, and most of the larger investigation. Full geographic reproduction requires the supplied geometry, its recorded demographic attributes and the matching rules. The exact Census/ACS vintage and table identifiers were not established from the inspected body, so a current Census download is not an exact substitute. If the attachment disappears, use a documented historical tract release and report changed boundaries/vintages and resulting counts.
data.caveats: The sensitivity output currently renders SyntaxError: Unexpected token, although its calculation definitions can be inspected. Its dynamic output was therefore not verified by moving the slider. Other analytical branches work. Distinguish unknown-race policies, source populations and matched denominators. Tract racial composition is contextual evidence, not the individual driver's race; the analysis does not supply a traffic-exposure baseline establishing causation.

examples.title: Local Spatial Autocorrelation Interactive Tutorial
examples.pattern: Neighbor definition → standardization → spatial lag → global/local inference

screenshots.caption: The narrative explains contiguity, a Queen/Rook control changes the neighbor definition, and an explicit connectivity calculation precedes the maps.
screenshots.crop_note: Browser side margins cropped; page content is unchanged.

screenshots.caption: Later linked investigation after selecting department 22, Côtes-du-Nord: the scatter, selected region and its neighbors connect the classification to its geographic context.
screenshots.crop_note: Browser side margins cropped; page content is unchanged.

screenshots.crop_note: Browser side margins cropped; page content is unchanged.

examples.story: Using Guerry’s charitable-donation data, the walkthrough asks which apparent concentrations in nineteenth-century France are statistically supported. It develops a global Moran statistic, then asks where the clusters occur. The illustrated low-low pattern lies in the south/southeast; a low-high example shows how one large neighbor can pull a neighborhood average upward. This is a worked statistical investigation, although its teaching purpose is prominent.
examples.prose_role: The prose defines each prerequisite, explains formulas and null-reference distributions, interprets quadrants and local classifications, then guides a linked selection back to its neighboring observations.

data.origin: The GeoDa Center’s Guerry collection, based on André-Michel Guerry’s 1833 study and additional historical sources; an 85-department WGS84 GeoJSON is attached.

links.label: Original researcher’s codebook and CSV links

data.grain: One of 85 historical French departments, with polygon geometry and 23 attributes. The collection spans 1815–1834; individual variables describe different periods rather than a common time series.
data.fields: dept (stable identifier), Dprtmnt (name), geometry and Donatns (default variable). The tutorial calls Donatns charitable donations per capita; the original codebook specifies donations to the poor but does not resolve the monetary unit/denominator. Derived z scores and spatial lags are dimensionless.
calculations: Choose Queen (shared vertex/border) or Rook (shared border) adjacency; row-standardize neighbor weights for weighted averages.
Visible standardize function uses ss.mean, ss.standardDeviation and ss.zScore; calculate spatial_lags with geoda.spatialLag(weights,std_vals).
Fit the spatial lag on standardized values; the source takes bestFit.slope as global Moran I. The observed default is approximately 0.353.

Generate permutation reference distributions and pseudo-p=(R+1)/(M+1). Local conditional permutations fix the selected location and shuffle other values. The live Local Moran call supplies weights, selected column, permutation count, lookup method and significance cutoff.
Local Moran values, pseudo-p values and quadrants feed class colors, counts, maps and selection details. Six natural-break classes provide the original-value map.
data.dependencies: Geometry → weights/connectivity; chosen variable → z scores → neighbor lags → scatter/global I. Weights + variable + permutations + threshold → local statistics → class counts/maps. Department selection links detail statistics, scatter and geographic neighbors.
data.reproducibility: Core methods and data are exposed, with substantive primary methodological documentation. No random-seed control was observed, so exact permutation outcomes should not be promised. Clicking Run changed the null-distribution mean from −0.013 to −0.010 while I remained 0.353 and pseudo-p 0.001.
data.caveats: Two live standalone cells display SyntaxError (the initial distribution/histogram cell and a standalone LISA-map cell), while the main neighbor map, permutation histograms, Moran scatter and later linked views render. The final linked scatter labels its x-axis standardized but displays raw-scale ticks; use the earlier correct standardized scatter for the analytical reproduction. The source workbook discusses multiple-comparison limitations; local classes are exploratory and depend on threshold/permutations.

sequence: Define the hotspot question → load departmental data → choose and inspect neighbor weights.
Choose the donation field → standardize → compute neighbor lag → explain the Moran scatter and global statistic.
Construct a permutation reference → compare observed I with randomized results → ask where clustering occurs.
Compute local statistics and classes → inspect a cluster map/table → select a department and examine its neighbors → interpret the relationship.

fit.minimum: Fix the Guerry field and Queen neighbors, retain the calculation chain and formulas, show the correct standardized scatter/I, a permutation histogram, and a local-results table plus one map. The bespoke linked two-map apparatus can be omitted. Precomputed statistics would reproduce a static story but would not test recalculation.
fit.compatible: Text, tables, calculated columns, controls, saved state and ordinary charts plausibly cover the presentation and inspection pieces. Spatial/statistical computation is a capability to investigate, not assumed.
fit.investigate: Neighbor relations or geometry support, grouped weighted calculations, global/local spatial statistics, randomized execution with repeatable state, explicit rerun controls, linked selection across blocks, and error propagation without obscuring functioning results.
fit.roundtrip: Axes and field mappings, thresholds, permutation count, binning, reference lines, class colors, map classification and selection keys should persist to text. A graphical change to a significance cutoff changes the derived classification, not merely its styling.
fit.scope: Weights and variable affect many downstream blocks; local significance/permutation settings affect local results and colors. A selected department changes the linked explanation and local simulator. The global Run refreshes its randomized reference result.
fit.lesson: This tests a deep dependency chain, the difference between changing a parameter and rerunning a stochastic calculation, and saving enough state to review a result. It also exposes the need to keep formulas, units, labels and dependent graphics synchronized.

examples.title: Is Seattle Really Seeing an Uptick In Cycling?
examples.pattern: Time series → confounder adjustment → residual trend

screenshots.caption: The opening data examination: Python aggregation cells, weekly directional totals and prose introducing a moving-average comparison in one reading column.
screenshots.crop_note: Geometric excerpt of the captured page; the uncropped capture is included in the ZIP.

screenshots.caption: A later dependent step: the correction formula, residual-variability output, corrected traffic chart and interpretation introducing the next rolling calculation.
screenshots.crop_note: Geometric excerpt of the captured page; the uncropped capture is included in the ZIP.

examples.story: The investigation asks whether apparent growth in Fremont Bridge bicycle traffic survives adjustment for daylight, weekday, and weather. It develops an author-reported historical estimate of roughly 10% annual growth in **bridge crossings**, not distinct cyclists or citywide ridership. Each paragraph explains why the preceding view is insufficient and introduces the next covariate or calculation. Visible Python cells make the progression from raw counts to adjustments unusually clear. The two captured regions demonstrate full reading-column blocks rather than a dashboard.
examples.prose_role: Each paragraph explains a limitation of the preceding view, introduces the next confounder or calculation, and interprets the resulting correction. Code cells remain visible between these decisions and their plots.

data.origin: Original data: Seattle's Fremont Bridge counter dataset and NOAA daily observations for SeaTac Airport station USW00024233. The article links NOAA's daily data search; that old service endpoint was not independently verified. The author's exact CSV snapshots were fetched and inspected.
data.grain: Crossing grain: one hour at one bridge, Date plus northbound and southbound count. Snapshot: 14,568 rows, October 2, 2012 through May 31, 2014. Counts are passages. Some directional counter cells are blank; the article has no explicit imputation block. Weather grain: station-day, 609 rows October 1, 2012 through June 1, 2014. Relevant fields DATE, TMIN and TMAX (tenths of °C), PRCP (tenths of mm). Other weather fields are unused. Code converts temperature to °F with 0.18*T+32 and rain to inches with PRCP/254, then joins by date.
data.fields: Crossing data: Date and Fremont Bridge NB/SB, hourly crossing counts; calculated total, day/week and weekday. Weather: DATE, TMIN/TMAX in tenths of °C, PRCP in tenths of mm, converted to °F/inches. Calculated daylight hours and elapsed-day count enter successive models.
calculations: Verified calculations: total = northbound + southbound; daily and weekly sums; 30-observation rolling mean; mean traffic by weekday; daylight-hours calculation from date, latitude 47.61° and axial tilt 23.44°; successive ordinary least squares models; predicted traffic; corrected series actual - prediction + mean(prediction). Later models add weekday indicators, daylight, minimum/maximum temperature, precipitation, then elapsed day count. The time coefficient is annualized relative to mean daily traffic.
data.dependencies: Dependency chain: hourly → daily → weekly/weekday summaries; date → daylight; daily + weather + weekday/daylight → fitted model → predictions → corrected traffic → 30-day rolling summary and final trend.
data.reproducibility: The data and visible methods are sufficient to reconstruct the exploratory sequence, with explicit decisions about missing counter values, window alignment, legacy pandas behavior, and statistical uncertainty.
data.caveats: Method caveats: prose describes a centered 30-day mean, but the code does not request centering; reproduce the code's right-aligned/trailing setting explicitly, or label a deliberate centered variant. Old pandas documentation indexing confirms center=False default; the exact archived HTML/PDF page could not be reopened, so avoid claiming an archived-document inspection. Current official rolling documentation likewise defines right-aligned default. The source's explicit coefficient covariance inversion includes all seven weekday dummy columns plus an intercept, making the design singular/unstable; a temperature-error calculation also omits covariance. Do not present the printed ±2% as independently validated. Fit/prediction views remain a strong workflow reference; uncertainty estimation requires review.

fit.compatible: Existing charts, tables, filters, calculated fields and saved state appear useful, based only on the product description.
fit.investigate: Date joins, ordered-window calculations, named intermediate datasets, fitted-model outputs and coefficient/result tables. Daylight can be supplied as a documented derived input for a smaller version. Statistical uncertainty requires methodological review because of the source covariance problems.
fit.roundtrip: Selected series, x/y encodings, temporal aggregation, window length and alignment, colors, legends, labels and axis limits should update the corresponding defining text. A chart appearance edit should not refit its model.
fit.scope: A source date filter affects every dependent summary/model/output. A smoother window affects only its smoother and explicitly dependent statements. Any proposed predictor control must name the model it changes; the original article has static outputs rather than analytical widgets.
fit.lesson: Named intermediate results and selective re-execution must preserve a long dependency chain while keeping prose attached to the result it interprets. No arbitrary-JavaScript requirement follows from this example.

examples.title: Get started with tidymodels and #TidyTuesday Palmer penguins
examples.pattern: Explore → fit and validate → revise the visual encoding

screenshots.caption: The first exploration: known-sex filtering and scatterplot code, a species-faceted result and interpretation before modeling.
The later model result: coefficient table and interpretation motivate changing the scatterplot x-axis from flipper length to bill depth while retaining the other encodings.

examples.story: Can body measurements and species predict a penguin's recorded sex? The article begins with an exploratory plot, compares two classification models, checks the selected model on held-out data, then uses its coefficients to revisit the visualization. Its argument has a useful return to an earlier analytical choice: bill depth separates recorded sexes better than the original x variable, after the model highlights that measurement. The prose gives each modeling step a purpose and distinguishes apparent separation from validation. It is a full code-and-result walkthrough, despite the introductory title.
examples.prose_role: Prose gives each modeling step a purpose, interprets held-out results and coefficients, then explains why an earlier axis choice should change. This distinguishes a visually plausible separation from a validated prediction and makes a concrete editing decision part of the argument.

data.origin: Original collectors: Kristen Gorman and Palmer Station LTER. Original species files: Adelie, Gentoo, Chinstrap. These links were obtained from the authors' data documentation; the tidy CSV itself was fetched and parsed.
data.grain: Row = one measured penguin, 344 records, three species, Biscoe/Dream/Torgersen islands in Antarctica's Palmer Archipelago, 2007–2009. Fields species, island, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, sex, year. Lengths in mm; body mass in grams.
data.fields: species, island, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, sex, year. Four numeric body measurements enter the model with species; island and year are dropped.
calculations: Filter missing sex: 333 usable records (168 male, 165 female), all complete on the four numeric features. The model drops island and year. The initial plot maps x=flipper length, y=bill length, color=sex, size=body mass, alpha=0.5, facet=species.

Seed 123; stratified train/test split by sex, visible output 250 training and 83 testing records. Twenty-five bootstrap resamples of training data compare a logistic GLM and ranger random forest, predicting sex from species plus four measurements. Resampling results are similar; the author selects the simpler logistic model.

Held-out model result reported by article: accuracy 0.940, ROC AUC 0.991. These are reproduced article outputs, not our newly validated estimates. Exponentiating coefficients gives odds ratios; the article interprets bill depth as particularly informative while flipper length has little additional evidence conditional on the other predictors.

The concluding plot changes x to bill depth and keeps the other encodings. Source code for all calculations and data is visible/available. Exact old-package random samples/results can vary with software versions.
data.dependencies: Source → known-sex rows → first and revised plots. Known-sex rows → seeded stratified split → training resamples → model comparison/selection → held-out predictions/metrics and coefficients. The coefficient interpretation motivates a visual revision, rather than mechanically changing the data.
data.reproducibility: The tidy CSV was fetched and parsed, with all 333 known-sex rows complete on the four numeric measurements. Inline R exposes all preparation, modeling and plotting steps; original species data links are documented.
data.caveats: The target is recorded sex, not species. Article model scores are reported outputs, not new validation by this research. Exact old-package resamples/results may differ with software versions. The optional video is not needed to recover the visible analysis.

Optional: random-forest comparison, 25 bootstraps, ROC traces, video and exact theme. Facets can be three vertically consecutive species charts.
Do not require omitted custom features for the core

This preserves a genuine prediction check; the random-forest comparison and 25-bootstrap exercise are optional.
fit.compatible: Filtering, interactive scatterplots, size/color controls, tables and calculated fields appear compatible with the stated capabilities. Facets could be three vertically consecutive species charts if needed.
fit.investigate: Faceting, logistic model fitting, predicted-class/probability outputs, held-out partitions, seeded resampling and model-result tables. The app description does not establish these capabilities.
fit.roundtrip: Graphical edits to x/y fields, color, size, opacity, facets and labels should update the block text. Changing a chart x-axis should not silently redefine the model predictor set.
fit.scope: Data-scope changes affect both visualizations and all model/validation descendants. A visual encoding change affects only that output. The original analytical walkthrough has no live model or chart controls; these editing controls are proposed.
fit.lesson: A model result can motivate revising an earlier chart without creating an execution cycle: both charts still depend on the filtered records, while the model provides editorial motivation. Keep analytical model definitions distinct from chart encodings.

examples.title: Many countries have decoupled economic growth from CO₂ emissions, even if we take offshored production into account
examples.pattern: Normalize time series → compare definitions → compare countries

screenshots.caption: The UK comparison: explanatory text, a three-series percentage-change chart with source notes and controls, followed by the next-country question.
An interaction actually performed: switch the same block to Table and search for United Kingdom. The table exposes raw units and percentage changes while retaining the narrative context.

examples.story: The article tests whether GDP can increase while carbon emissions fall, then considers the objection that a country may simply have moved emissions abroad. The UK comparison puts economic output, territorial emissions and consumption-based emissions on a common relative-change scale. The narrative then asks readers to inspect other countries before distinguishing national progress from inadequate global progress. Prose defines the metrics, anticipates an objection, interprets the result, and guides the next comparison. The main two figures are full-width sequential blocks; the later country-facet image is optional, not a dashboard requirement.
examples.prose_role: Prose defines production and consumption emissions, anticipates the objection that emissions have moved abroad, interprets the UK result, asks readers to inspect other countries, and separates national progress from the global conclusion.

data.origin: Original sources: World Bank GDP per capita PPP indicator, sourced to Eurostat/OECD/IMF/World Bank (2026); Global Carbon Budget (2025); OWID population sources (2024). Download metadata explicitly documents per-capita calculation and carbon-to-CO₂ conversion.

links.label: World Bank GDP per capita PPP indicator

data.grain: Row = entity-year; current download has 8,622 rows, 242 countries/regions, years 1990–2025. Fields Entity, Code, Year, GDP per capita, CO₂ emissions per capita, Consumption-based CO₂ emissions per capita. Nulls and series endpoints differ.
data.fields: GDP unit is international dollars at 2021 prices (inflation and purchasing-power adjusted). Emissions are tonnes CO₂/person, fossil fuels and industry; land-use change is excluded. Consumption emissions = production emissions − embedded exports + embedded imports, then divide by population.
calculations: GDP unit is international dollars at 2021 prices (inflation and purchasing-power adjusted). Emissions are tonnes CO₂/person, fossil fuels and industry; land-use change is excluded. Consumption emissions = production emissions − embedded exports + embedded imports, then divide by population.

Displayed normalization: relative change from 1990. Our explicit check 100*(value_t/value_1990−1) on downloaded values agrees with the displayed UK endpoints: GDP +61.02% (2025), territorial emissions −56.87% (2024), consumption emissions −38.91% (2023). Those endpoints are different years; do not describe all three as a 2025 comparison. Exact Grapher behavior for missing baseline data was not inspected.
data.dependencies: Entity-year prepared metrics → country selection → per-series 1990 baseline lookup → normalized series → line comparison/table. Repeat for other countries using the same source/definitions. Preserve the raw levels separately from percentage-change outputs.
data.reproducibility: The actual full-data download, metadata and README were inspected, and the relative-change calculation was checked against the displayed UK endpoints. The exact prepared dataset and documented definitions suffice for the article-level investigation. Reconstructing the underlying trade-embedded emissions estimates from raw trade data is outside this reference.
data.caveats: Displayed normalization: relative change from 1990. Our explicit check 100*(value_t/value_1990−1) on downloaded values agrees with the displayed UK endpoints: GDP +61.02% (2025), territorial emissions −56.87% (2024), consumption emissions −38.91% (2023). Those endpoints are different years; do not describe all three as a 2025 comparison. Exact Grapher behavior for missing baseline data was not inspected. The newer article charts should be reproduced from this exact download, not automatically from the convenient owid/co2-data repository: its GDP series/units can differ.

fit.investigate: Group-relative lookup of baseline values, preserving nulls and different series endpoints, explicit denominator/baseline scope, and chart/table controls that consistently name their affected data.
fit.roundtrip: Selected measures and countries, baseline year, date range, colors, percentage-axis formatting, annotations and line-end labels should update the corresponding text definition.
fit.scope: Country/date selections must state whether they apply to one output or a shared group of blocks. In the inspected source, switching the UK chart to Table initially exposed all 242 entities; a table search was needed to isolate the UK. That observed scope mismatch is informative.
fit.lesson: Baseline transforms and alternate metric definitions should be inspectable beside the chart. A country change can invalidate a country-specific prose conclusion, so execution/state needs to distinguish fixed editorial examples from reader-selected results. The central calculation does not require a general statistical runtime.

examples.title: Film Dialogue from 2,000 screenplays, Broken Down by Gender and Age
examples.pattern: Grouped shares → within-film ranks → age comparison → drilldown

screenshots.caption: The Disney comparison: gender word-share bars followed by interpretation and the qualification that screenplays do not exactly transcribe the completed films.
screenshots.crop_note: Geometric excerpt of the captured page; the uncropped capture is included in the ZIP.

screenshots.caption: A later analytical step: age at film release is explained before a word-weighted age comparison and its interpretation.
Optional interaction evidence: selecting Reservoir Dogs changes the adjacent character-word breakdown. The explorer is more dashboard-like than the main essay and need not define the notebook layout.

examples.story: The essay moves from a familiar subset (Disney) to all films, asks whether having a female lead changes total dialogue balance, then examines how words are distributed across actors' ages. The distinction between a lead character and all supporting dialogue is the analytical turn: a story can center a woman while most words still go to male characters. Prose also exposes the measurement limits before asking readers to explore individual films. This is a visual essay with calculations described in prose rather than visible code cells. The first graphic has three groups and the age graphic two facets, but each is one sequential analytical block; the optional final explorer is more dashboard-like.
examples.prose_role: Prose starts with a familiar subset, introduces measurement limits immediately after the first result, distinguishes lead roles from the contribution of the whole cast, motivates the age question, and then invites individual-film inspection.

data.origin: Original material is screenplays found online, character matching to IMDb actor/actress entries, and actor age at film release. The public source-matching spreadsheet is linked by the article but not inspected. Original copyrighted screenplay texts are not provided as a complete downloadable corpus.
data.grain: Character grain: one matched screenplay character; 23,048 rows, fields script_id, imdb_character_name, words, gender, age. Age is the actor's age, not the character's. Words, not lines, is the central count despite the HTML page title mentioning lines. Film grain: one screenplay/film, 2,000 rows, script_id, imdb_id, title, year, gross, lines_data. Actual CSV film years span 1929–2015. Join on script_id. The public core CSV does not include genre or a Disney flag. Domestic gross is described as inflation-adjusted, but unit/base year was not verified.
data.fields: Character data: script_id, imdb_character_name, words, gender, age (actor age at release). Film data: script_id, imdb_id, title, year, gross, lines_data. Gender is a binary coding with five unknown rows. Join on script_id; genre and Disney membership are absent from these core files.
calculations: Published filtering: characters with at least 100 words are matched; the article says at least 90% of a script's lines are assigned by gender. Minimum word count in released character CSV is 101. Small roles and script-to-screen changes affect individual-film results.

Necessary transformations are transparent conceptually: sum words by film and gender, divide by film total for share; rank characters by words within film; count female lead/second/top-three roles; group actor ages and sum words. Our independent check of released rows gives 436 female leading-word characters out of 2,000 films (21.8%), consistent with the article's rounded 22%.
data.dependencies: Character rows + film metadata → joined table → grouped word totals/share denominator and within-film ranks. Those feed film summaries. Cleaned actor ages feed a separate word-weighted age view. Selected script_id filters the character detail.
data.reproducibility: The data suffice for film shares, character ranks and a documented exploratory age variant. They do not reproduce the initial extraction, exact genre filters, or the original age calculation without further source work. Suitable substitute: use the released aggregate CSVs, select Disney films by an explicitly listed title set, omit genre/gross filters, report cleaned-age coverage.
data.caveats: Exact original chart code, tie policy, unknown-gender denominator and age-cleaning rules were not verified. Released data has five “?” gender rows, 4,785 NULL ages and 16 implausible ages above 110 (some values resemble release years). These need an explicit cleaning rule; do not silently reproduce the age percentages as exact. Displayed age bins are “Under 21,” “22 to 31,” “32 to 41,” “42 to 65,” “65+”; exact inclusive endpoints are ambiguous without code.

elements: Define word count, threshold and script limitations
Sum words by film/gender; normalized share; sort
Subset tabs observed; exact Disney membership needs definition
Contrast lead character with total cast dialogue
Descending rank within film; counts by rank/gender
Explicit age bins; word-weighted sum and within-gender denominator

documented aggregation/denominator, film share comparison, rank contrast, method caveats. Optional: age section until cleaning is settled; custom Disney typography; all-film animated transitions; narrow tooltip layout; exact genre/gross filters; approximate dialogue timeline.
Do not require omitted custom features for the core

fit.minimum: A named film subset with normalized gender shares → all-film share summary → lead/rank comparison → film selection with character contributions. Conventional stacked bars and tables preserve the argument.
fit.compatible: Tables, interactive charts, filters and calculated fields appear suitable for the aggregate-data core. Custom Disney styling and film graphics are unnecessary.
fit.investigate: Joining character and film records, ranking/top-k inside groups, linking film selection to its character rows, and keeping percentage denominators explicit when filters change. Age reproduction also requires an explicit cleaning/coverage policy.
fit.roundtrip: Grouping fields, normalization, sort order, gender colors, the 50% reference, selected films, filter predicates and labels should update defining text.
fit.scope: A selected film drives its character detail. A broader subset changes shares/rank summaries only in explicitly connected blocks. In the source, narrative summaries stay fixed while the optional explorer changes. Genre controls are observed, but the released core CSV lacks genre.
fit.lesson: A visual filter can accidentally alter the denominator of a percentage. This reference tests aggregate-to-detail lineage, within-group ranking and the difference between fixed narrative examples and scoped exploratory selections.

recommendations.title: What's different? Timeseries forecast performance
recommendations.scope: Keep a source table, actual-versus-forecast line chart, a named delta = actuals − forecast calculation, a signed difference chart, one event annotation and the interpretation connecting them.
recommendations.test: This isolates the central promise: a small textual calculation feeds multiple full-width outputs, while graphical changes to encodings, the zero line, colors and annotation persist to the appropriate block's text.
recommendations.reason: The dataset is already prepared and the arithmetic is transparent. A useful first proof can be small without losing the argument. Resolve the source's inconsistent power/energy labels before presenting a polished reproduction.

recommendations.title: Discovering Date Patterns
recommendations.scope: Preserve raw-data inspection, a rolling time series, local calendar-field derivation, a derived table and a selectable grouped comparison.
recommendations.test: This exercises reusable intermediate data, ordered windows, timezone semantics and multiple control scopes. A facet edit changes the grouping configuration and dependent group means; a local brush should retain its declared scope.
recommendations.reason: It combines the kinds of tables, calculations, filters and graphical editing already described for explorEDA. The two local calculation branches make it a stronger workflow test than simply placing several charts beneath paragraphs.

recommendations.title: Is Seattle Really Seeing an Uptick In Cycling?
recommendations.scope: Preserve the count summaries, weather/date join, one explicitly specified adjustment model, predictions and corrected series, with a qualified interpretation.
recommendations.test: This tests joins, model-result tables, dependent calculations and selective re-execution. Cosmetic chart edits must remain distinct from changing a predictor, a training/data scope or a derived quantity.
recommendations.reason: The analytical argument depends on each preceding calculation, while the graphics remain conventional. Reproduce the reasoning structure first; review the legacy model specification and uncertainty calculation before treating its historical numerical estimate as validated.
